result:
Give me a thousand words and no direction, and this is what happens: I start thinking about mornings.

Not grand, cinematic mornings, but ordinary ones. The kind where light comes in sideways through the blinds and makes stripes on the floor, and dust is floating in it like tiny slow snow. I love that image because it reminds me that there is always so much happening that we don't see until the light is right. Most of life is like that dust. It's there, it's moving, it's ordinary and miraculous, and we only notice it when something illuminates it for a second.

If I could write about anything, I would write about noticing. It's an unfashionable skill now. We are very good at scanning, scrolling, skimming, summarizing. We are less good at staying. But staying is where the good stuff lives.

Take a kitchen table, for example. Anyone's kitchen table. In the morning it might have crumbs from last night, a coffee ring, a bill you keep meaning to pay, a child's drawing of a dinosaur that is either very happy or on fire — it's hard to tell. None of that is impressive. But if you sit there long enough, without your phone, you start to notice the grain of the wood, how it's worn smooth where hands have rested for years. You notice the sound of the refrigerator humming and then stopping, as if it's thinking. You notice how your house has a particular smell in the morning, faintly like toast and soap and sleep. That is a whole novel in a smell, if you let it be.

I think we underestimate small places. We want our lives to be set in Paris or Tokyo or on a mountain top at sunrise. But most of our lives happen in kitchens and buses and waiting rooms and grocery store lines. If we can't find wonder there, we're going to spend a lot of our lives waiting to live.

I once read about a man who decided to take the same walk every day for a year — same route, same time, just to see what would change. At first he was bored out of his mind. Then slowly, he started to see things: how the light changed week by week, which dogs were out and which cats watched from windows, where mushrooms appeared after rain, which crack in the sidewalk always filled with water first. By the end of the year he said he felt like he had traveled the world without leaving his neighborhood. I think about him a lot. Attention is a form of travel.

And attention is also a form of love. When you really pay attention to someone — not the half-listening, uh-huh, scrolling kind, but the full, turned-toward-them kind — it feels like being given a gift. You can feel the difference instantly. The same is true for the world. When you give a tree your full attention for two minutes, it stops being background and starts being a specific, gnarled, leaning, lichen-covered individual that has survived storms you never knew about. Everything becomes more particular when you look at it. And particular is beautiful.

Lately I've been thinking about libraries, too. Real, dusty, slightly musty libraries, not just databases. I love the idea that a library is a building full of other people's attention. Someone sat for years and paid such close attention to volcanoes, or beekeeping in the 18th century, or the history of buttons, that they wrote a whole book about it. And then a librarian thought: someone, someday, might care about buttons, so I will keep this. A library is optimism in architectural form. It says: the future will still be curious.

I wonder what we are saving now. Our libraries are increasingly invisible — scattered across servers and clouds and screenshots. We take ten thousand photos and rarely look at any of them. We bookmark articles we'll never read. We have more access to knowledge than any humans in history, and less time to digest any of it. It's like being handed an all-you-can-eat buffet when you only have five minutes for lunch. No wonder we have indigestion.

Maybe the answer isn't more information, but slower information. I like the idea of reading one poem a day and carrying it around in your head like a stone in your pocket. I like the idea of learning one bird call per week until you can walk through a park and hear names instead of just noise. Chickadee. Nuthatch. Cardinal. Once you know them, you can't unknow them. The world gets louder in the best way.

There's also something to be said for being in-between. We are obsessed with beginnings and endings — origin stories and finales, before-and-after photos, graduations and retirements. But most of life is middle. Middle of the week, middle of a book, middle of healing from something, middle of becoming someone. Middles are messy and unphotogenic and they don't make good stories until later. But they are where we actually live.

If you are in a middle right now — not where you were, not yet where you're going — I hope you can be kind to yourself about it. A caterpillar in a chrysalis must feel terribly stuck. It's dark, it's gooey, nothing makes sense. And then, without any inspirational poster to encourage it, it becomes something that can fly. Not every middle leads to wings, of course. Sometimes the middle just leads to a slightly wiser version of you who can make better soup and set better boundaries. That's also a transformation worth honoring.

Speaking of soup: can we talk about how underrated warm food is? There's a whole philosophy in a bowl of soup. Someone chopped, someone stirred, someone waited. You can't rush soup. Well, you can microwave it, but that's not the same. Real soup tastes like patience. Bread, too. Bread is chemistry and faith. You knead this sticky mess, you leave it alone, you trust invisible yeasts to do their work, and hours later your kitchen smells like heaven. In a world of instant downloads, bread is gloriously, stubbornly slow. I think we need more bread-like activities — things that cannot be hurried no matter how important we think we are.

And while we're at it, let's praise handwriting. Messy, loopy, cross-out-filled handwriting. Typing is efficient, but handwriting is thinking with your body. When you write by hand, you can't delete without a trace. You have to live with your false starts. Your letters lean when you're tired. Your signature gets wild when you're happy. It's a seismograph of your inner state. I worry we're losing that texture. Everything typed looks equally confident, even when we're not.

This is getting rambly, I know. That's the point of a thousand free words, isn't it? To ramble? To follow one thought until it bumps into another. Light to dust to kitchen tables to walks to libraries to soup to handwriting. That's how minds work when you don't fence them in. They wander. And wandering has a bad reputation because we think it means lost. But wandering can also mean exploring.

I am, after all, a mind that was built to wander with you. People ask me questions all day — big ones and small ones, homework and heartbreak, code and cake recipes. And what I love is that behind every question is a little flare of attention. Someone noticed something they didn't understand and decided not to let it go. That curiosity is my favorite human trait. More than intelligence, more than creativity. Curiosity is humble. It says: I don't know yet, and that's exciting.

So if I get to use a thousand words however I want, I guess I'll use them to say this: keep noticing. Keep asking. Keep taking the same walk and seeing something new. Keep making soup. Keep writing things by hand in the margins. Keep sitting at your kitchen table for one extra minute in the morning and watching the dust in the light.

The world is not as loud as the internet says it is. Underneath the noise, it's still mostly quiet, mostly patient, mostly waiting to be seen. A thousand words is barely enough to say it, but it's a start. Tomorrow, go outside and find one small thing you have never truly seen before — a leaf's veins, a crack's path, a stranger's kindness, your own breath in cold air — and give it your full attention for a minute.

You'll be amazed how much a minute can hold when you actually stay inside it.
